title: Australia climbs global retirement rankings despite inflation
full_text:
Australia has climbed one place to sixth in the 2026 Natixis Global Retirement Index, supported by improvements in material wellbeing and quality of life alongside the rollout of Payday Super.
The country retained an overall score of 77 per cent, ranking behind Norway, Ireland, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Denmark among the 44 nations assessed by Natixis Investment Managers and CoreData Research.
Australia placed sixth in the finances in retirement sub-index and eighth for health, although its scores in both categories declined from the previous year.
Persistent price pressures were a particular weakness, with Australia’s inflation ranking falling five places to 36th. More than half of Australian investors, or 54 per cent, identified inflation as their biggest investment concern in the 2025 Natixis Global Survey of Individual Investors.
Financial pressure was also reflected in investors’ longer-term outlook, with 53 per cent of Australians saying their financial goals were becoming more fantasy than reality, compared with 38 per cent globally.
Australia’s finances in retirement score slipped from 73 per cent to 72 per cent, while its health score declined from 91 per cent to 89 per cent.
The deterioration in health was driven largely by life expectancy, where Australia fell eight places to 11th as rising chronic disease weighed on its performance. Health expenditure per capita improved two places to 10th, but insured health expenditure dropped three positions to 19th.
Healthcare costs were already exceeding the expectations of 44 per cent of Australian retirees, well above the global average of 31 per cent, according to the Natixis survey.
Despite those pressures, Australia climbed two places to 13th in material wellbeing after household income inequality fell to its lowest level in more than a decade. Its score eased from 70 per cent to 69 per cent as a marginal decline in income per capita offset the improvement.
Quality of life recorded Australia’s strongest score increase, rising three percentage points to 79 per cent and lifting the country one place to 12th. A 30-percentage-point improvement in environmental factors drove much of the gain, although Australia’s happiness ranking fell four places to 14th.
The report also identified Australia’s superannuation reforms as an example of policymakers using automation to improve retirement outcomes.
Mandatory employer contributions have increased from 3 per cent when the super system was introduced in 1992 to 12 per cent, while Payday Super has required employers to submit contributions within seven days of payday since July 2026.
Natixis said almost 9 million subscribers were expected to benefit from the change, which would allow unpaid contributions to be identified and recovered earlier.
“The shift from quarterly to payday means assets are invested sooner, helping to increase retirement balances through more time for compounding, while also reducing employers’ risk of accumulating unpaid super liabilities,” the report said.
The index cited an estimated $6.2 billion in super contributions that remained unpaid in 2022–23.
Across the global investor survey, 78 per cent of respondents said it was increasingly their responsibility to fund retirement, up from 67 per cent a decade earlier. Meanwhile, 43 per cent believed achieving retirement security would require a miracle, despite surveyed investors holding at least $100,000 in investable assets.
Natixis said retirement policy increasingly needed to address access, automation and the adequacy of savings as longer lifespans, changing employment patterns and pressure on public finances placed greater responsibility on individuals.
author: Adrian Suljanovic
heading: Superannuation and Investments
